0001-teozalcoalco.title: Pintura de Teozacoalco (JGI XXV-03)
0001-teozalcoalco.caption: A map of Teozacoalco, created by an unknown Mixtec artist at the request of King Phillip II of Spain.
0001-teozalcoalco.creditLine: Joaquín García Icazbalceta Manuscript Collection, Benson Latin American Collection, LLILAS Benson Latin American Studies and Collections, The University of Texas at Austin
0001-teozalcoalco.digitizedLine: Digitized by the University of Texas Libraries
0001-teozalcoalco.source: Benson Latin American Collection, The University of Texas at Austin
0001-teozalcoalco.altText: A colorful, circular aerial view of a map depicting various roads, rivers, buildings, and people spread out amidst mountain ranges. To the left of the map are two columns of drawings of people that indicate the various types of interactions between different groups, which are located sporadically within the circle. There are also other icons resembling plant and animal life as well as different types of edifices (churches, castles) lining the circle’s edge.

0004-table.title: Table 1.1
0004-table.artist: Stuard Card, Jock Mackinlay, and Ben Shneiderman
0004-table.caption: The hierarchical definition of visualization provided in Stuard Card, Jock Mackinlay, and Ben Shneiderman’s influential visualization textbook, Readings in Information Visualization: Using Vision to Think (Morgan Kaufman, 1999).
0004-table.altText:
A table of definitions describing the layers of cognitive processing and design required for visualization. From top to bottom, the categories read as follows: 

External Cognition: Use of the external world to accomplish cognition.
Information design: Design of external representations to amplify cognition.
Data graphics: Use of abstract, nonrepresentational visual representations of data to amplify cognition.
Visualization: Use of computer-based, interactive visual representations of data to amplify cognition.
Scientific visualization: Use of interactive visual representations of scientific data, typically physically based, to amplify cognition.
Information visualization: Use of interactive visual representations of abstract, nonphysically based data to amplify cognition.
0004-table.cleanCaption: The hierarchical definition of visualization provided in Stuard Card, Jock Mackinlay, and Ben Shneiderman’s influential visualization textbook, Readings in Information Visualization: Using Vision to Think (Morgan Kaufman, 1999).

0005-reprorights.caption: “After Roe Fell: Abortion Laws by State,” an interactive visualization of abortion access across the United States, in which the degree of access is mapped to a five-color scale. 0005-reprorights.altText: A webpage that color-coordinates the states of the United States according to abortion access. 0008-deardata.title: A Week of Clocks
0008-deardata.caption: [ SEE ABOVE ]
0008-deardata.altText: The back and front of a postcard. The front depicts an illustration of arrows, lines, and dots forming a snowflake-like figure. The top left corner reads “a week of clocks,” and the top right indicates Stefanie is the postcard’s artist. On the back, Giorgia Lupi is the addressee (though her specific street address is scribbled over in pen), and the left provides a key of the front’s drawing. After a brief greeting to Giorgia, Stefanie explains the symbols behind her sketch. Each line symbolizes one hour of the day, moving clockwise, and each segment represents a day of the week. She further explains the types of arrows and points that correspond to phone, laptop, tablet, watch, microwave, car, oven, and church clock usage.

0012-anon.title: Graph of planetary movements, given as an illustration to a short appendix, titled De cursu per zodiacum, to a copy of Macrobius' Commentary on Cicero's Somnium Scipionis
0012-anon.caption: Two prominent examples of proto-data visualizations, first surfaced by Howard Funkhauser in 1937 and (justifiably!) celebrated through the present day. Little is known about the image on the left, an anonymous tenth-century diagram of the changing locations of constellations in the night sky. On the right is a set of fourteenth-century charts of the relationships between quantities created by French philosopher Nichole Oresme.
0012-anon.creditLine: Printed in H. Gray Funkhouser, "A note on a tenth century graph", Osiris 1 (1936), p. 260.
0012-anon.altText: A line graph of the solar system charting the movements of constellations. The y-axis is written in Spanish and lists eight celestial bodies. Underneath each name is a slower or sun-like sketch, except for the last, which is of a crescent moon. From top to bottom, they are: Venus, Mecur (Mercury), Saturn, Sol (Sun), Mars, Luppré (Pluto), and Luna (Moon).

0014-plot.altText: A vertically-oriented line chart divided into twelve sections—six on top and six on the bottom—for each month of the year that shows daily barometric pressure. The lines for the months of January through June occupy the top half of the page, and July through December take up the bottom half of the page. The title reads, “Philosoph. Transact. Numb. 169.” Numbers 1 through 31 are vertically listed next to each line to the right of every month’s section.

0016-playfair.title: "Chart of all the import and exports to and from England from the year 1700 to 1782"
0016-playfair.caption: William Playfair's "Chart of all the import and exports to and from England from the year 1700 to 1782"
0016-playfair.altText: A line graph of Playfair’s showing the imports and exports to and from England from 1700 to 1782. The top red line represents exports and the lower yellow line represents imports, both showing a slight and steady increase as they move down the x-axis. The area between the two lines is shaded in blue and represents the balance in favor of England. Once the lines reach the year 1770, vertical lines for the last twelve years until 1782 are printed, which also coincides with a sharper decrease in both imports and exports.

0017-halley.title: "An Historical Account of the Trade Winds, and Monsoons, Observable in the Seas between and near the Tropicks, with an Attempt to Assign the Phisical Cause of the Said Wind"
0017-halley.caption: Edmond Halley’s “Map of the Trade Winds,” which appeared in a pamphlet published by the Royal Society in 1686.
0017-halley.altText: A map of the southern hemisphere of the globe with the African continent in the center. Trade winds are depicted by segmented lines over bodies of water. Some lines are clustered closer together than others, especially towards the top of the map, closer to the equator. The major bodies of water demarcated are the Indian Ocean, the Æthiopic Ocean, and Atlantick Ocean.
